analysis.one_liner: Permanently eliminates the federal estate tax on large inherited fortunes.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the estate tax died in the House Ways and Means Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have eliminated the federal estate tax permanently, so that no estate would ever pay tax on inherited wealth again. It also keeps the rule that inherited assets are revalued at current market prices when the owner dies, so heirs never pay capital gains tax on decades of appreciation either. The bill was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Heirs of the largest estates. In 2011, the estate tax applied only to the portion of an estate above the exempt amount, roughly $5 million per person, so a full repeal is worth the most to families passing on fortunes of many millions or more. Those heirs would owe nothing to the Treasury on the transfer, and under the bill's basis provision they would also escape capital gains tax on the growth in value of inherited assets.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals chapter 11 of the Internal Revenue Code, eliminating the estate tax for anyone dying after December 31, 2010 [S2] [S3].

It retains stepped-up basis at death, meaning heirs re-inherit assets at their current market value and never owe capital gains tax on the appreciation that accumulated during the original owner's lifetime [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Everyone else, indirectly. The estate tax is one of the few federal taxes paid only by very large fortunes; eliminating it removes that revenue permanently, which must be made up through borrowing, other taxes, or cuts to public programs [S2].

drawbacks.text: Because the estate tax falls almost entirely on estates large enough to exceed the roughly $5 million exemption, repeal is a tax cut concentrated on the wealthiest families, and the revenue loss adds to the deficit or shifts the burden to other taxpayers [S2].

Combined with the bill's retention of stepped-up basis, repeal means billions in capital gains on inherited assets would never be taxed by anyone, creating a permanent break for wealth held across generations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits go to a small group — heirs of estates exceeding the multimillion-dollar exemption — while the cost is permanent revenue loss spread across all taxpayers. A full repeal with stepped-up basis retained leaves large inherited fortunes essentially untaxed at transfer and untaxed at sale, which is the most favorable treatment of inherited wealth available under the tax code.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there for the rest of the Congress; it was never voted on by the committee or either chamber.

narrative.text: Representative Latta introduced the bill on January 5, 2011, the first week of the new Congress [S1] [S5].
It was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that writes tax law [S5].
The committee never reported the bill and neither chamber ever voted on it; the action history shows no activity after the referral [S5].
The bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, without a final outcome [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The federal Treasury, and everyone else who would otherwise have had to make up roughly the revenue now paid by estates above the multimillion-dollar exemption. Heirs of very large estates, who stood to save the most from repeal, are the ones worse off that the bill died.

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the estate tax repeal bill on the first day of bill filings in the new Congress.

for.name: 32 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill, giving it a small bloc of support in the majority's chamber.

for.name: 1 House Democrat
for.what_they_did: Crossed the aisle to cosponsor the repeal.

against.name: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Chair of the tax-writing committee (Republican majority)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for committee consideration, so it sat in committee from January 2011 until the Congress ended.

against.name: House leadership
against.role: Majority leadership that sets floor scheduling
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote in two years.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 33 cosponsors were overwhelmingly Republican — 32 Republicans and just 1 Democrat — and no vote was ever taken, so the fight never really went to the floor.

industries.industry: Heirs and families of very large estates
industries.note: Repeal would eliminate the estate tax that currently applies only to estates above the roughly $5 million exemption, plus preserve the stepped-up basis break so inherited gains are never taxed. The cost is permanent lost federal revenue borne by other taxpayers.

industries.industry: Estate planning lawyers and wealth advisory firms
industries.note: A permanent repeal would shrink the market for estate tax planning, but it would also make the rules simpler and more predictable for wealthy clients. Either way, the industry's interests revolve around how much tax large fortunes owe.

industries.industry: Family farms and small business owners
industries.note: Repeal proponents argue these businesses face estate tax pressure; however, under 2011 law the roughly $5 million exemption already shielded most such estates from the tax, so the benefit for them is far smaller than for the largest fortunes.
